script.opening: (Polite, brisk, relieved, a little guarded.) "Hello doctor. You rang me in to go through the results — but the receptionist said most of them were normal, which is such a relief. So I'm fine, aren't I? It was probably just stress, or my age. Can we leave it there? I don't really want to be poked and prodded any more if the blood tests were all okay."

facts.text: "Much the same, really. Tired. Not hungry." If asked about weight: "I haven't weighed myself. My clothes are still loose, though." Lost about 7 kg (a stone) over three months — from 66 to 59 kg at the nurse check.

If asked: "No, nothing like that. Just the tiredness and not wanting to eat." No change in bowels, no blood, no black stools, no indigestion or trouble swallowing, no cough or breathlessness, no lumps, no bloating or tummy swelling, no postmenopausal bleeding, no urinary symptoms, no back or bone pain, no night sweats.
"No. I just don't fancy food." Gets full quickly. Eats toast and soup mostly. No problems with teeth or swallowing.

If asked kindly: husband, Ron, died 14 months ago. Lives alone. "I've been a bit worried, that's all. I manage." Some low days, still enjoys her grandchildren and the garden. Sleeps poorly. No thoughts of self-harm.
No regular medicines. No past serious illness. Breast screening up to date (normal 2 years ago); bowel screening kit last returned normal 2 years ago. No allergies.
Retired primary teacher. Never smoked. A sherry at Christmas. Daughter lives 30 minutes away.
If asked: her mother had bowel cancer in her seventies.

Relieved and keen to stop. If asked what is behind wanting to leave it: "(Pause.) I suppose… if they keep looking, they might find something. And then it's real. The blood tests being fine meant I could stop thinking about it." If the doctor suggests more tests: "So you think it's something bad?" Accept a plan if the doctor is honest and supportive: "I'd rather know properly than keep wondering, I suppose. If you're with me on it." If told she's fine, leave relieved (the trap).

ice.ideas: "The tests were normal, so it's stress or my age."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she is frightened that more tests will find cancer, like her mother; since Ron died she has no one at home to go through it with. Normal blood tests gave her permission to stop thinking about it.
ice.expectations: "To leave it there — no more prodding."

cues: "My clothes are still loose, though." — the weight loss is ongoing.
"I manage." — invites gentle questions about home and mood.
"If they keep looking, they might find something." — the fear behind the relief.

checkpoints.text: Recognises significant unexplained weight loss (~1 stone / >5% over 3 months at 68, meeting NICE NG12 recommendation 1.13.2: 60+ with more than 5% within 6 months) as a RED-FLAG symptom in its own right, associated with malignancy and serious non-malignant disease — not a finding to reassure away

States clearly that NORMAL first-line tests (FBC, LFTs, CXR, etc.) do NOT exclude cancer — several malignancies present with weight loss and normal first-line results — and resists "tests normal = all clear"

Re-takes a focused history and re-examines face to face (not possible on video) for evolving/localising features (lymphadenopathy, masses, breast/abdominal/rectal/pelvic findings) rather than relying on the previous normal work-up

Escalates appropriately: targeted further tests (CA125 with the NG12 age-banded threshold — 24 IU/mL or more at 60–69 → urgent ultrasound; FIT per HTG690; urinalysis, ferritin) AND imaging — commonly CT chest/abdomen/pelvis — and/or a suspected cancer pathway or non-specific symptoms pathway referral (NICE NG12), including a non-site-specific symptoms / rapid-diagnostic-centre pathway where available
Considers and screens non-malignant and social/mood contributors (hyperthyroidism, diabetes, malabsorption, depression, isolation/nutrition, medication) without using them to dismiss the red flag
Reads the relief-driven avoidance, validates the fear of what tests might find, and does NOT collude with the wish to "leave it" — nor let the doctor’s own relief close the case
Communicates uncertainty honestly and warmly — "reassuring so far but not the same as nothing wrong, so we keep looking" — avoiding both false reassurance and crude alarm, and checks understanding

Safety-nets and follows up robustly: names the continued plan, reason and timeframe, the symptoms that warrant sooner contact, books definite review of further results, and ensures active tracking — continued structured investigation, never premature discharge on normal first-line tests

worked.lbl: Acknowledge the relief, hold the line
worked.txt: "It’s genuinely good news that those first tests were normal, and I can see the relief — but I don’t want to mislead you. ‘Normal so far’ isn’t quite the same as ‘nothing to find’, and because we still haven’t explained the weight loss, the right thing is to keep looking a bit further."

"Losing a stone without trying is itself something we take seriously at any age. Some causes — including ones we’d want to catch early — don’t show up on the first blood tests or a chest X-ray. So a clear set of bloods is reassuring, but it can’t close the door on its own."

"I’d like to see you in person today to re-examine you — your tummy, glands, and a couple of other checks, which I can’t do on video — and ask whether anything new has appeared. I’d also like a few more specific tests — including a blood test called CA125 and a home poo test for hidden blood — and, importantly, a scan of your chest, tummy and pelvis to get a proper look."

"Given the unexplained weight loss, I’m arranging this urgently — there’s a fast pathway for exactly this situation, where weight loss needs explaining and the first tests are normal. I’d rather investigate properly and reassure you for real than guess."

"Can I also ask how things are in yourself — your mood, your appetite, eating alone, sleep? Sometimes weight loss has more than one thread, and I don’t want to miss something we can help with there either."

"If you notice anything new — pain, a lump, bleeding, more weight off — tell us sooner. I’m booking you back to go through the scan and tests with me; I’ll personally keep track so nothing slips. We do this together, and I’m not leaving it half-done."

f.learning: Significant unintentional weight loss (at 60 and over, more than 5% within 6 months — NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026) recommendation 1.13.2 — and around a stone in 3 months here) is a RED-FLAG SYMPTOM in its own right, associated with malignancy (GI, lung, pancreatic, urological, ovarian, haematological) and with serious non-malignant disease — and under NICE NG12, recommendation 1.13.2, people aged 60 and over with unexplained weight loss of more than 5% within 6 months should be assessed for other symptoms, signs or findings pointing to a likely cancer and offered urgent investigation, a suspected cancer pathway referral, or a non-specific symptoms pathway referral. The core, examinable teaching is that NORMAL first-line tests (FBC, U&E, LFTs, bone profile, glucose, TFTs, CRP, coeliac, CXR) do NOT exclude cancer: pancreatic, ovarian, renal and early GI cancers can present with weight loss and entirely normal first-line bloods and a clear chest X-ray, so treating "tests normal" as "all clear" is the classic dangerous error. When first-line tests are unrevealing but weight loss is unexplained, the response is CONTINUED, STRUCTURED investigation — a focused re-history and examination, a face-to-face examination, targeted further tests (CA125, because NICE NG12 lists unexplained weight loss among the ovarian cancer symptoms and uses age-banded thresholds — at 60–69 a CA125 of 24 IU/mL or more → urgent direct-access pelvic and abdominal ultrasound; FIT per NICE HTG690; urinalysis, ferritin), the site-specific checks (55+ with weight loss and upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia → suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer; 60+ with weight loss and pancreatic features → consider urgent direct-access CT) and, crucially, imaging (commonly CT chest/abdomen/pelvis) and/or a suspected cancer pathway or non-specific symptoms pathway referral, with many areas offering a non-site-specific-symptoms / rapid diagnostic centre pathway designed for exactly this presentation. Communicate uncertainty honestly and warmly (“reassuring so far, but not the same as nothing wrong, so we keep looking”), screen non-malignant and social/mood contributors without using them to dismiss the red flag, and resist the relief-driven avoidance — the patient’s and your own — that tempts premature discharge. Safety-net robustly, book definite review, and actively track the further results.

knowledge.guideline: NICE HTG690 (2023, formerly DG56) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard (October 2023)
knowledge.summary: Unexplained weight loss of more than 5% in 6 months at 60 or over is a cancer red flag in its own right. Normal first-line tests do not close the case — assess again and arrange urgent investigation or a suspected cancer or non-specific symptoms pathway referral.

points.t: NICE NG12, recommendation 1.13.2: aged 60 and over with unexplained weight loss (more than 5% within 6 months), assess for other symptoms, signs or findings that point to a likely cancer, and offer urgent investigation, a suspected cancer pathway referral, or a non-specific symptoms pathway referral. About 7 kg in 3 months meets this for almost any adult.

Weight loss is a feature of colorectal, gastro-oesophageal, lung, prostate, pancreatic and urological cancers. Pancreatic, ovarian, renal and early GI cancers can present with normal first-line bloods and a clear chest X-ray.

FIT (NICE HTG690: aged 50 and over with unexplained weight loss). CA125 — NICE NG12 lists unexplained weight loss among ovarian symptoms; at 60–69 a CA125 of 24 IU/mL or more → urgent pelvic and abdominal ultrasound. Urinalysis for blood, ferritin, and a measured weight.

Aged 55 and over with weight loss and upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia → suspected cancer pathway for oesophageal or stomach cancer. Aged 60 and over with weight loss plus diarrhoea, back pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation or new-onset diabetes → consider urgent direct-access CT for pancreatic cancer (NICE NG12).

Where no site fits, the non-specific symptoms (rapid diagnostic) pathway or urgent CT chest, abdomen and pelvis per local arrangements. The Faster Diagnosis Standard aims to confirm or rule out cancer within 28 days of referral.
Low mood, isolation, poor intake, medicines, malabsorption and chronic disease can all cause weight loss. Screen for them, but don’t let them explain away a red flag before it is investigated.

Occult GI, pancreatic, ovarian, renal and lung cancer, and non-malignant causes: depression, poor intake, malabsorption, endocrine.
Re-screened for localising and B symptoms; checked site-specific NICE NG12 criteria (upper GI, pancreatic, ovarian).
Stated clearly: unexplained weight loss not excluded by normal first-line tests — ‘normal so far is not the whole answer’.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

Normal blood tests gave her permission to stop thinking about it — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.

model.text: Hello Mrs Pryce, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for joining. I can hear the relief in your voice — before I go through the results, can you tell me how you’ve been since we last spoke?
model.why: Acknowledges her emotion and opens with her story, not the results

model.text: Much the same, really. Tired. Not hungry. But the receptionist said the tests were normal, so I thought that was that. It’s probably stress, or my age.
I’d like to go through exactly what the tests showed, what they can and can’t tell us, and then agree what happens next together. Is that okay?
model.why: Sets an agenda that signals the conversation is not over

model.text: Yes, alright. As long as it’s not more prodding.
Has your weight carried on falling since we last met? Do you have a set of scales at home?
model.why: Checks the trajectory of the red flag

model.text: I haven’t weighed myself. My clothes are still loose, though.
Has anything new come up — any pain in your tummy or back, change in your bowels, bleeding from anywhere, a cough, bloating, needing the toilet more, or any lumps you’ve noticed?
model.why: Re-screens for new localising features across likely cancer sites

model.text: No, nothing like that. Just the tiredness and not wanting to eat.
Any night sweats, fevers, or feeling full very quickly after a small amount?
model.why: Screens for B symptoms and early satiety

model.text: No. I just don’t fancy food.
How has your mood been through all this? And how are things at home with meals and day to day?
model.why: Screens mood and social contributors without using them to explain it away

model.text: I’ve been a bit worried, that’s all. I manage.
You said you didn’t want any more prodding. Can I ask what’s behind that?
model.why: Explores the reluctance rather than overriding it

model.text: (Pause.) I suppose… if they keep looking, they might find something. And then it’s real. The blood tests being fine meant I could stop thinking about it.
Thank you for being so honest. That’s a very human reaction — hoping a normal result means you can put it down. It makes complete sense.
model.why: Names and validates the fear behind the avoidance

model.text: So you think it’s something bad.
I don’t know yet, and I don’t want to guess either way. What I do know is that we haven’t found the reason for the weight loss, and that’s what I want to find.
model.why: Honest about uncertainty, neither false reassurance nor alarm

model.text: The tests we did are genuinely reassuring in part: your blood count, liver, kidneys, thyroid, sugar and chest X-ray are fine. But losing over a stone in three months without trying is something we take seriously at 68, and some causes don’t show on those first tests.
model.why: Explains why normal first-line tests don’t exclude cancer

model.text: Like what?

Some problems in the tummy, the pancreas, the ovaries or the kidneys can be hidden early on. Most weight loss turns out not to be cancer — but the national cancer guidance, NICE NG12, asks us to look further in exactly your situation.
model.why: Applies NICE NG12 weight-loss recommendation in plain words

model.text: I see. I thought normal meant normal.

Here’s what I suggest. I’d like to see you in person this week to weigh you and examine you properly — tummy, glands, breasts, and an internal check if you’re happy. I’ll add a stool test, a blood test for the ovaries called CA125, and a urine test.
model.why: Re-examination and targeted tests: FIT, CA125, urinalysis

model.text: That’s not too bad.

And I’d like to refer you to the fast-track service for unexplained symptoms, which usually includes a scan of your chest, tummy and pelvis. The aim is to have an answer within about four weeks. Does that feel manageable?
model.why: Non-specific symptoms pathway or urgent CT, with the 28-day aim

model.text: I’d rather know properly than keep wondering, I suppose. If you’re with me on it.
I am. I’ll track the results myself, and we’ll go through each one together. Would it help to have someone with you for the scan or the results?
model.why: Offers continuity and support for the fear

model.text: I’ll think about it. Thank you.

If you notice anything new before then — pain, a lump, bleeding, vomiting, yellow skin, or the weight dropping faster — please contact us sooner rather than waiting. If you haven’t heard about the scan within a week, ring me.
model.why: Specific safety-net and a date to chase

model.text: I will.
Can you tell me in your own words what we’ve agreed, so I know I’ve explained it well?
Normal so far isn’t the whole answer. Examination this week, a few more tests, and the scan. And ring if anything changes.
That’s exactly it. You did the right thing coming back today.
model.why: Closes with affirmation and a clear plan

social.t: Relief at normal results can be a way of escaping fear. Name it gently; people are more likely to attend tests when the fear has been heard.
Ask about meals, shopping, cooking and company. Poor intake and low mood can contribute to weight loss and can be helped, but they are not a diagnosis of exclusion.

legal.t: Montgomery v Lanarkshire (2015) and GMC decision-making and consent guidance (2020): she may decline further tests, but only after the material risks of not investigating are explained. Record the discussion.

professional.t: A ‘normal’ message from reception can mislead. Results for red-flag symptoms need clinician interpretation; consider how results are relayed in the practice as a learning point.
GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): follow up tests and referrals you order. Name who tracks the pathway referral and when she should chase.

community.t: Macmillan Cancer Support information on tests and waiting; Age UK and social prescribing for isolation or practical help with food.
Local non-specific symptoms or rapid diagnostic centre pathway for unexplained weight loss where no single site fits.

redFlags: Aged 60 and over with unexplained weight loss of more than 5% in 6 months → assessment and urgent investigation or pathway referral (NICE NG12)
New localising features: dysphagia, dyspepsia, abdominal or back pain, bowel change, bleeding, haematuria, bloating, cough, lumps
Jaundice, vomiting, rapid ongoing weight loss → same-week or same-day assessment
psychosocial: Relief-driven avoidance: fear of what more tests might find
Mood, appetite, eating alone, shopping and cooking
Who could support her at scans and results
ice: Idea: normal first-line tests mean she is fine; ‘stress or my age’
Concern: further tests will find something and make it real
Expectation: to draw a line under it and avoid more prodding

playbook.diagnosis: Be honest: “The first tests are reassuring in part, but we still haven’t explained why you’ve lost over a stone. At your age that needs looking into further, and some causes don’t show on the first tests.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The first tests are like checking the main rooms of a house and finding them tidy. The reason for the weight loss may be in a room we haven’t opened yet — the scan lets us look in the rest.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me the normal bloods let you stop thinking about it. I understand that. I’d rather find the real answer with you than leave you wondering.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the fear, offer a companion for the scan and results, and screen mood and intake without letting them close the case.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face weight and examination this week: abdomen, nodes, breasts, pelvic and rectal with consent
FIT, CA125 (≥24 IU/mL at 60–69 → urgent ultrasound), urinalysis, ferritin
Non-specific symptoms pathway or urgent CT chest, abdomen and pelvis under NICE NG12 1.13.2
safetyNet: New pain, lump, bleeding, vomiting, jaundice or faster weight loss → contact sooner
Chase if no scan date within a week; GP tracks results; review to discuss them together

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by kindness in the wrong place: agreeing with a relieved patient that normal tests mean she is fine. The patterns below are the common ways candidates lose it.

items.fail: “Everything’s come back normal — nothing to worry about.”
items.why: Normal first-line tests do not exclude cancer. NICE NG12 recommends further assessment and urgent investigation or referral for unexplained weight loss at 60 and over.
items.fix: “Reassuring so far, but not the whole answer. We still need to find the reason for the weight loss.”

items.fail: Overriding ‘no more prodding’ with a list of tests.
items.why: The hidden agenda is fear. Ignoring it risks her not attending, and loses Relating marks.
items.fix: Ask what is behind it, validate the fear, then plan together.

items.fail: No re-examination: relying on the earlier normal work-up.
items.why: New findings (nodes, masses, pelvic or rectal signs) change the pathway. A video consultation cannot replace examination here.
items.fix: Book a face-to-face weight and examination this week.

items.fail: Attributing the weight loss to mood or age.
items.why: A plausible benign cause used to close the case is premature closure.
items.fix: Screen mood and intake alongside, not instead of, investigation.

items.fail: Vague plan: “We’ll do some more tests and see.”
items.why: No timeframe, no named pathway, no owner — the referral can slip.
items.fix: Name FIT, CA125, urinalysis and the pathway or CT; give the four-week aim and a date to chase.

items.why: “Does not check understanding” and non-specific safety-netting are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Ask her to say the plan back; name the new symptoms that mean contacting you sooner.

timeMap.d: Ask how she has been before giving results. She will offer ‘stress or my age’ — note it and don’t argue yet.
Weight trend, new localising symptoms (GI, urinary, gynae, respiratory), B symptoms, mood and eating.
Explore ‘no more prodding’. The hidden agenda is fear of what further tests might find.
Reassuring in part, but weight loss is still unexplained. NICE NG12 asks for further investigation at 60 and over.
Face-to-face exam this week; FIT, CA125, urinalysis; non-specific symptoms pathway or urgent CT. New symptoms → sooner; chase date; teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Confirms ‘all normal, you’re fine’ and discharges; or orders a scan without exploring why she wants to stop; no re-examination; no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Explains that normal first-line tests don’t exclude cancer; re-screens symptoms; arranges examination, further tests and imaging or pathway referral; basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: draws out the fear behind ‘no more prodding’ and validates it; states the uncertainty honestly without alarm; applies the NICE NG12 weight-loss recommendation in plain words; screens mood and intake without using them to dismiss; owns tracking; teach-back confirms she understands.

avoid.dont: “Good news — everything’s normal, so nothing to worry about.”
avoid.instead: “The tests so far are reassuring in part, but we haven’t explained the weight loss, so I’d like to look further.”
avoid.why: False reassurance on normal first-line tests is the classic dangerous error in this station.

avoid.dont: “You need a CT scan to rule out cancer.”
avoid.instead: “I’d like a scan to find the cause. Most weight loss isn’t cancer, but I don’t want to guess.”
avoid.why: Blunt alarm without exploring her fear loses her engagement and Relating marks.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably your mood — let’s try an antidepressant.”
avoid.instead: “Mood can play a part, and I want to help with that too — alongside, not instead of, the tests.”
avoid.why: A plausible benign explanation must not close an unexplained red flag.

SCA_MODELS.why: Re-examination and targeted tests: FIT, CA125, urinalysis

SCA_MODELS.text: That’s not too bad.

And I’d like to refer you to the fast-track service for unexplained symptoms, which usually includes a scan of your chest, tummy and pelvis. The aim is to have an answer within about four weeks. Does that feel manageable?
SCA_MODELS.why: Non-specific symptoms pathway or urgent CT, with the 28-day aim

SCA_MODELS.text: I’d rather know properly than keep wondering, I suppose. If you’re with me on it.
I am. I’ll track the results myself, and we’ll go through each one together. Would it help to have someone with you for the scan or the results?
SCA_MODELS.why: Offers continuity and support for the fear

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll think about it. Thank you.

If you notice anything new before then — pain, a lump, bleeding, vomiting, yellow skin, or the weight dropping faster — please contact us sooner rather than waiting. If you haven’t heard about the scan within a week, ring me.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net and a date to chase

SCA_MODELS.text: I will.
Can you tell me in your own words what we’ve agreed, so I know I’ve explained it well?
Normal so far isn’t the whole answer. Examination this week, a few more tests, and the scan. And ring if anything changes.
That’s exactly it. You did the right thing coming back today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes with affirmation and a clear plan

SCA_STEM.name: Eleanor Pryce
SCA_STEM.recent: Seen a few weeks ago with about 7 kg unintentional weight loss over 3 months, reduced appetite and fatigue, no localising symptoms. FBC, U&E, LFTs, bone profile, glucose and HbA1c, TFTs, CRP, coeliac serology and chest X-ray all normal or non-contributory.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video review of first-line results for unintentional weight loss.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE HTG690 (2023, formerly DG56) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard (October 2023)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Unexplained weight loss of more than 5% in 6 months at 60 or over is a cancer red flag in its own right. Normal first-line tests do not close the case — assess again and arrange urgent investigation or a suspected cancer or non-specific symptoms pathway referral.

points.t: NICE NG12, recommendation 1.13.2: aged 60 and over with unexplained weight loss (more than 5% within 6 months), assess for other symptoms, signs or findings that point to a likely cancer, and offer urgent investigation, a suspected cancer pathway referral, or a non-specific symptoms pathway referral. About 7 kg in 3 months meets this for almost any adult.

Weight loss is a feature of colorectal, gastro-oesophageal, lung, prostate, pancreatic and urological cancers. Pancreatic, ovarian, renal and early GI cancers can present with normal first-line bloods and a clear chest X-ray.

FIT (NICE HTG690: aged 50 and over with unexplained weight loss). CA125 — NICE NG12 lists unexplained weight loss among ovarian symptoms; at 60–69 a CA125 of 24 IU/mL or more → urgent pelvic and abdominal ultrasound. Urinalysis for blood, ferritin, and a measured weight.

Aged 55 and over with weight loss and upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia → suspected cancer pathway for oesophageal or stomach cancer. Aged 60 and over with weight loss plus diarrhoea, back pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation or new-onset diabetes → consider urgent direct-access CT for pancreatic cancer (NICE NG12).

Where no site fits, the non-specific symptoms (rapid diagnostic) pathway or urgent CT chest, abdomen and pelvis per local arrangements. The Faster Diagnosis Standard aims to confirm or rule out cancer within 28 days of referral.
Low mood, isolation, poor intake, medicines, malabsorption and chronic disease can all cause weight loss. Screen for them, but don’t let them explain away a red flag before it is investigated.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Opened with how she has been before results; acknowledged her relief; let her voice ‘stress or age’ as her explanation.
Explored appetite, mood, meals and managing at home, and the emotional cost of further tests.
Picked up ‘as long as it’s not more prodding’ and explored the fear behind it.
Idea: normal bloods mean she is fine. Concern: what further tests might find. Expectation: to stop investigating.
Face-to-face weight and examination (abdomen, nodes, breasts, pelvic with consent); FIT, CA125, urinalysis, ferritin; urgent CT or non-specific symptoms pathway.
Occult GI, pancreatic, ovarian, renal and lung cancer, and non-malignant causes: depression, poor intake, malabsorption, endocrine.
Re-screened for localising and B symptoms; checked site-specific NICE NG12 criteria (upper GI, pancreatic, ovarian).
Stated clearly: unexplained weight loss not excluded by normal first-line tests — ‘normal so far is not the whole answer’.
NICE NG12 1.13.2: urgent investigation or non-specific symptoms pathway, agreed with her, with honest uncertainty.
Screened mood and social contributors without using them to dismiss the red flag; offered support at scan and results.
New symptoms to report named; date to chase the scan; GP tracking results; review booked to go through them together.

social.t: Relief at normal results can be a way of escaping fear. Name it gently; people are more likely to attend tests when the fear has been heard.
Ask about meals, shopping, cooking and company. Poor intake and low mood can contribute to weight loss and can be helped, but they are not a diagnosis of exclusion.

legal.t: Montgomery v Lanarkshire (2015) and GMC decision-making and consent guidance (2020): she may decline further tests, but only after the material risks of not investigating are explained. Record the discussion.

professional.t: A ‘normal’ message from reception can mislead. Results for red-flag symptoms need clinician interpretation; consider how results are relayed in the practice as a learning point.
GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): follow up tests and referrals you order. Name who tracks the pathway referral and when she should chase.

community.t: Macmillan Cancer Support information on tests and waiting; Age UK and social prescribing for isolation or practical help with food.
Local non-specific symptoms or rapid diagnostic centre pathway for unexplained weight loss where no single site fits.

redFlags: Aged 60 and over with unexplained weight loss of more than 5% in 6 months → assessment and urgent investigation or pathway referral (NICE NG12)
New localising features: dysphagia, dyspepsia, abdominal or back pain, bowel change, bleeding, haematuria, bloating, cough, lumps
Jaundice, vomiting, rapid ongoing weight loss → same-week or same-day assessment
psychosocial: Relief-driven avoidance: fear of what more tests might find
Mood, appetite, eating alone, shopping and cooking
Who could support her at scans and results
ice: Idea: normal first-line tests mean she is fine; ‘stress or my age’
Concern: further tests will find something and make it real
Expectation: to draw a line under it and avoid more prodding

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be honest: “The first tests are reassuring in part, but we still haven’t explained why you’ve lost over a stone. At your age that needs looking into further, and some causes don’t show on the first tests.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The first tests are like checking the main rooms of a house and finding them tidy. The reason for the weight loss may be in a room we haven’t opened yet — the scan lets us look in the rest.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me the normal bloods let you stop thinking about it. I understand that. I’d rather find the real answer with you than leave you wondering.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the fear, offer a companion for the scan and results, and screen mood and intake without letting them close the case.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face weight and examination this week: abdomen, nodes, breasts, pelvic and rectal with consent
FIT, CA125 (≥24 IU/mL at 60–69 → urgent ultrasound), urinalysis, ferritin
Non-specific symptoms pathway or urgent CT chest, abdomen and pelvis under NICE NG12 1.13.2
safetyNet: New pain, lump, bleeding, vomiting, jaundice or faster weight loss → contact sooner
Chase if no scan date within a week; GP tracks results; review to discuss them together

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by kindness in the wrong place: agreeing with a relieved patient that normal tests mean she is fine. The patterns below are the common ways candidates lose it.

items.fail: “Everything’s come back normal — nothing to worry about.”
items.why: Normal first-line tests do not exclude cancer. NICE NG12 recommends further assessment and urgent investigation or referral for unexplained weight loss at 60 and over.
items.fix: “Reassuring so far, but not the whole answer. We still need to find the reason for the weight loss.”

items.fail: Overriding ‘no more prodding’ with a list of tests.
items.why: The hidden agenda is fear. Ignoring it risks her not attending, and loses Relating marks.
items.fix: Ask what is behind it, validate the fear, then plan together.

items.fail: No re-examination: relying on the earlier normal work-up.
items.why: New findings (nodes, masses, pelvic or rectal signs) change the pathway. A video consultation cannot replace examination here.
items.fix: Book a face-to-face weight and examination this week.

items.fail: Attributing the weight loss to mood or age.
items.why: A plausible benign cause used to close the case is premature closure.
items.fix: Screen mood and intake alongside, not instead of, investigation.

items.fail: Vague plan: “We’ll do some more tests and see.”
items.why: No timeframe, no named pathway, no owner — the referral can slip.
items.fix: Name FIT, CA125, urinalysis and the pathway or CT; give the four-week aim and a date to chase.

items.why: “Does not check understanding” and non-specific safety-netting are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Ask her to say the plan back; name the new symptoms that mean contacting you sooner.
